briefs.bs-fever-rash-arthralgia:
Fever and Rash in a Child

vesicles in crops, a face-first spread, or hives mid-course of an antibioticWhat is the lesion, where did it start, how did it relate to the fever, and what exposure came before it?

DiagnosisPracticeWorkup and management
Bottom line

Name the lesion first; of the head-to-toe exanthems only varicella is vesicular, and hand-foot-and-mouth vesicles center on the palms, soles and mouth. Then ask where it started and how it related to the fever; when joints hurt too, date the rash against the exposure.

  • Varicella: itchy vesicles in successive crops, several stages side by side, from the scalp, face or trunk to the limbs. Up to date at age 3 is one of two doses (12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years), so milder breakthrough varicella, with lower fever and fewer lesions, stays on the list.
  • Measles: ill, with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis; a confluent maculopapular rash from the face down.
  • Rubella: fine pink rash from face to feet within 24 hours, palms and soles spared, posterior auricular and suboccipital nodes; unvaccinated and well. In teenage girls and women, finger and wrist pain may last up to a month. The MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine prevents measles and rubella.
  • Serum sickness-like reaction: itchy hives, low fever, nodes and tender but unswollen joints 5 to 14 days into a drug (penicillins, cefaclor, TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)). Stop the drug; it resolves. More common in children than serum sickness, and milder.
  • Serum sickness: same timing after a foreign protein (antivenom, antitoxin, monoclonal antibody), with high fever and low complement.
  • Acute rheumatic fever: swollen, hot, migratory joints, carditis or erythema marginatum 2 to 4 weeks after an untreated sore throat (extremely rare after prompt penicillin).

Sexual history decides two rashes: pustules with tenosynovitis (gonococcus) and a rash on the palms and soles (secondary syphilis).

Practice
  1. 5-year-old girl, 2 days of itching and low fever papules and blisters in crops on scalp and back one crusted lesion; two small blisters on a palm Had only her 12-month vaccines; recent travel T 38.0 °C · mouth normal → Varicella → itchy papules and blisters in crops on the scalp and trunk, a crusted lesion beside fresh ones (several stages at once), are varicella; one of two vaccine doses leaves room for milder breakthrough disease: supportive care. Two palm blisters do not make hand-foot-and-mouth disease, which centers on the palms, soles and mouth; roseola is never vesicular and appears as the fever breaks; the travel is a decoy
  2. 4-year-old girl whose parents declined vaccines has 3 days of fever cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes then a maculopapular rash from hairline to trunk small gray-white spots on a red buccal base T 40.0 °C · ill appearing → Measles → high fever with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, a face-first rash and Koplik spots in an unvaccinated, ill child is measles: airborne precautions, and vitamin A for severe measles. Rubella is mild with posterior nodes, and roseola appears as the fever breaks
  3. 6-year-old girl has bright red cheeks that spare the nasolabial folds lacy pink rash on arms and thighs, brighter after a warm bath Runny nose and low-grade fever last week; no sore throat; vaccines up to date Afebrile · well appearing → Erythema infectiosum → slapped cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds, then a lacy rash that comes and goes with heat, after a cold-like prodrome has passed, is erythema infectiosum from parvovirus B19; she is no longer contagious. Rubella is a face-first maculopapular rash with posterior nodes, and scarlet fever is sandpaper with a sore throat
  4. 6-year-old boy, 2 days of fever, itchy spreading rash sore wrists and ankles strep throat 9 days ago; oral penicillin ends tomorrow Hives on arms and back T 38.8 °C · nodes: neck, axillae, groin · joints tender, not swollen or red → Serum sickness-like reaction → hives with tender, unswollen joints and nodes 5 to 14 days into a drug is a serum sickness-like reaction: stop the penicillin; rheumatic fever has swollen migratory joints and is extremely rare after treated strep, and scarlet fever has no hives or joint pain
  5. 7-year-old girl from abroad has no vaccine records Low-grade fever, runny nose for 2 days pink, discrete maculopapules spread from face to limbs within a day tender posterior auricular, suboccipital nodes; eyes, buccal mucosa normal T 37.9 °C · well appearing → Rubella → a mild illness with discrete pink spots spreading from the face within a day and posterior auricular and suboccipital nodes is rubella; the MMR vaccine prevents it. Measles is confluent, with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots, and erythema infectiosum begins with slapped cheeks
  6. 8-year-old healthy boy whose family declined vaccines has never had chickenpox A classmate developed chickenpox 3 days ago No chronic illness or immune problem His parents ask how to protect him now Afebrile · no rash → Varicella vaccine now → a healthy, nonimmune child aged 1 or older gets varicella vaccine within 3 days, and possibly up to 5 days, of exposure, which can prevent or soften the illness. Immune globulin is for people at high risk who cannot receive the vaccine, and observation alone is for a child who is already immune
  7. 12-year-old boy, 1 day of fever and sore throat fine sandpaper rash on neck and trunk, darker in elbow creases strawberry tongue; pale skin around the mouth Tender anterior neck nodes; no conjunctivitis T 38.9 °C · HR 104/min → Scarlet fever → a fine sandpaper rash with flexural lines, circumoral pallor, a strawberry tongue and tender anterior nodes with a sore throat is scarlet fever, the one bacterial exanthem among the classic six: confirm with a rapid strep antigen test or throat culture, then penicillin or amoxicillin. Scalded skin syndrome begins with tender erythema and flaccid bullae in an infant or child under 5, and classic Kawasaki disease needs 5 or more days of fever plus 4 of 5 criteria; he has had 1 day and no conjunctivitis
  8. 16-year-old girl, unvaccinated, pink maculopapular rash since yesterday face first, now trunk, limbs; palms, soles spared finger, wrist pain since this morning; tired; no stiff neck inconsistent condom use Postauricular, suboccipital nodes; clear throat T 38.2 °C · well · rash blanches → Rubella virus → a fine rash from face to limbs within a day, sparing palms and soles, with posterior auricular and suboccipital nodes and finger arthralgia in an unvaccinated, well teenager is rubella; gonococcal pustules rarely reach the face, and measles makes the patient ill with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, without joint pain
  9. 7-year-old boy had bright red cheeks 3 days ago now a lacy pink rash on his arms and legs No chronic illness; playful His mother asks when he can return to school Afebrile → Return to school now → children with parvovirus B19 are no longer contagious once the rash appears, because the rash is immune mediated, so he can return now. Keeping him home until the rash fades protects no one, and the diagnosis is clinical, so no antibody test is needed first
  10. 14-year-old boy, 10 days after antivenom for a rattlesnake bite urticarial rash for 2 days knee and wrist pain, worse with movement Feels unwell; no wheeze or lip swelling T 39.5 °C · urine protein 2+ · serum complement low → Serum sickness → high fever, hives, joint pain and low complement 5 to 14 days after a foreign protein is serum sickness: immune complexes against the antivenom
  11. 3-year-old boy, 6 days of fever; vaccines up to date red eyes without discharge; cracked red lips; strawberry tongue swollen red hands, feet; polymorphous truncal rash One 2-cm anterior neck node; tonsils without exudate; rapid strep negative T 39.8 °C → Kawasaki disease → 5 or more days of fever with 4 of 5 features (nonexudative conjunctivitis, lip and oral changes, rash, extremity changes, a cervical node over 1.5 cm) and negative strep testing is Kawasaki disease: intravenous immunoglobulin and high-dose aspirin, then echocardiography. Scarlet fever has an exudative throat, and measles brings cough, coryza and Koplik spots
  12. 6-year-old girl with acute lymphoblastic leukemia is on chemotherapy Her brother developed chickenpox 7 days ago Her antibody test for chickenpox is negative Her parents ask what she needs now Afebrile · no rash → Varicella-zoster immune globulin now → an immunocompromised child without immunity cannot receive the live vaccine; she gets varicella-zoster immune globulin as soon as possible, within 10 days of exposure. Observation leaves her at risk of severe varicella
  13. 11-year-old boy with 5 days of fever hot, swollen right knee, then left elbow as the knee settles sore throat 3 weeks ago, not treated Faint, non-itchy pink rings with clear centers on trunk T 38.6 °C · ASO titer elevated → Acute rheumatic fever → migratory polyarthritis and erythema marginatum 2 to 4 weeks after untreated pharyngitis, with strep evidence, is acute rheumatic fever; Lyme arthritis is a single large joint months after erythema migrans
  14. 3-year-old girl has 2 days of low-grade fever and itchy blisters in crops on the trunk, face and scalp, some crusted No chronic illness; playful and drinking well T 38.0 °C → Supportive care with an oral antihistamine → a healthy child with uncomplicated varicella gets supportive care with an antihistamine. Oral acyclovir is not recommended for otherwise healthy children with typical varicella; it is for high-risk patients or complicated disease. Immune globulin is postexposure prophylaxis, not treatment
  15. 15-year-old girl, never vaccinated, with a fine pink rash began on the face; reached the legs within a day palms and soles spared; sore finger joints Suboccipital nodes; oropharynx clear T 38.0 °C · no conjunctivitis or cough → Rubella IgM serology → a face-to-feet rash within a day with suboccipital nodes and finger arthralgia in an unvaccinated teen is rubella: confirm with rubella IgM
  16. 7-year-old girl on day 8 of amoxicillin for otitis media 1 day of itchy wheals on trunk, limbs ankle and wrist pain, worse with movement; joints not swollen No wheeze; lips and tongue normal T 38.1 °C · blood pressure normal → Stop amoxicillin and give an oral antihistamine → a serum sickness-like reaction: stop the amoxicillin and give an oral antihistamine; epinephrine only for airway, breathing or blood-pressure compromise
  17. 4-year-old boy has had chickenpox for 4 days Most lesions have crusted, but two new blisters appeared on his trunk this morning His parents ask when he can return to day care Afebrile · eating well → Keep him home until every lesion has crusted → varicella is contagious from 1 to 2 days before the rash until every lesion has crusted, so new blisters keep him home. The fever settling does not end contagion, and covering the blisters does not make return safe
  18. 17-year-old girl, 3 days of fever pain over the backs of both wrists and hands with finger extension painful, swollen right knee Five small pustules on forearms and ankles T 38.4 °C · sexually active, no condoms · vaccinations up to date → Disseminated gonococcal infection → tenosynovitis, a few pustules and a swollen knee in a sexually active teen is disseminated gonococcal infection: aspirate the knee, NAAT of genital, pharyngeal and rectal sites, blood cultures, then ceftriaxone
  19. 5-year-old boy who finished amoxicillin for otitis media 6 days ago raised, nonblanching purple spots on buttocks and legs painful, swollen ankles Colicky abdominal pain T 37.9 °C · platelet count normal → IgA vasculitis → palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs with normal platelets, joint pain and colicky abdominal pain is IgA vasculitis, not a drug reaction: check a urinalysis
How NBME framed it: question 1

10-year-old girl, new to the United States from Central America with her family Vaccine history not given Five days of fatigue, mild itching all over, a low-grade fever and a slightly runny nose Rash for 1 day: began on the face, now covers the whole body No diarrhea or abdominal discomfort T 37.8 °C discrete maculopapules on face, trunk, back and limbs no lesions in the eyes or mouth

Which vaccine is most likely to have prevented her illness?

Competing answers
  • Varicella: itching and a whole-body rash suggest chickenpox; but her lesions are discrete maculopapules with no vesicles, and varicella needs vesicles in crops.
  • Typhoid: fever and a rash in a child from Central America suggest typhoid rose spots; but she has no abdominal pain or diarrhea, and her rash began on the face and covers the whole body.
  • Influenza virus: fever, fatigue and a runny nose fit influenza; but influenza does not typically cause a rash.
  • Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis: a routine childhood vaccine a recent immigrant may have missed; but diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis do not cause a spreading maculopapular rash.
  • Haemophilus influenzae type b: another routine vaccine she may have missed; but this organism causes epiglottitis, meningitis and pneumonia, not a face-first rash.
  • Hepatitis B: a routine infant vaccine she may have missed; but acute hepatitis B brings right upper quadrant pain and nausea, and she has no abdominal symptoms.
  • Inactivated poliovirus: a routine vaccine she may have missed abroad; but polio causes flaccid paralysis, not a rash.
  • Pneumococcal: a routine childhood vaccine she may have missed; but pneumococcus causes otitis media, pneumonia and meningitis, not a viral exanthem.

Down to two: measles-mumps-rubella or varicella. Measles-mumps-rubella: a face-first maculopapular rash that spreads down is measles or rubella, and the MMR vaccine prevents both, so the lead-in skips the diagnosis. The low fever, discrete spots and clear eyes and mouth fit rubella better than measles; the NBME explanation teaches measles, but the stem sets the facts. The options were the routine childhood vaccines plus one travel vaccine, typhoid.

Workup and management
By situation Serum sickness-like reaction – stop the drug if still taken; antihistamine and NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs); avoid the drug afterward; epinephrine only for airway, breathing or blood-pressure compromise · Rubella – supportive care (no specific antiviral), NSAIDs for the joints; contagious from 7 days before to 7 days after the rash, so isolate for 7 days after it appears; keep away from pregnant contacts (miscarriage, stillbirth, congenital rubella syndrome) · Measles – contagious from 4 days before to 4 days after the rash appears; isolate for 4 days after the rash; airborne precautions in health care settings, with a respirator (N95) and an isolation room; vitamin A for severe measles, and it may be given to any child with measles under a clinician's supervision · Erythema infectiosum – no longer contagious once the rash appears, because the rash is immune mediated; the child can stay in school · Viral exanthems – diagnosis is clinical; serology or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is for severe or atypical cases
Varicella: care and contagion Supportive care with antihistamines for a healthy child; oral acyclovir is not recommended for otherwise healthy children with typical varicella. Acyclovir is for high-risk patients or complicated disease: oral may be considered for healthy people older than 12 years, chronic skin or lung disease, long-term salicylates, or short, intermittent or aerosolized corticosteroid courses, and by some experts in pregnancy. Oral therapy works best when started within 24 hours of the rash; intravenous for immunocompromised patients or severe disease (pneumonia, encephalitis). A newborn whose mother's varicella began within 5 days before or 2 days after delivery needs varicella-zoster immune globulin and acyclovir, as prophylaxis or treatment. A prodrome of fever and malaise may come 1 to 2 days before the rash, but in children the rash is often the first sign. Contagious from 1 to 2 days before the rash until every lesion has crusted, so keep the child home and use airborne and contact precautions until then. Complications: secondary bacterial skin infection (the commonest cause of hospitalization), pneumonia, encephalitis. Diagnosis is clinical; PCR of a vesicle only when the picture is atypical.
Varicella postexposure Immune – prior chickenpox or 2 vaccine doses: observe only · Not immune, immunocompetent – age 1 or older and not pregnant: varicella vaccine within 3 days, and possibly up to 5 days, of exposure; after day 5 give it anyway for future protection, but it no longer prevents this infection · Not immune and high risk – immunocompromised, pregnant, a newborn whose mother's rash began 5 days before to 2 days after delivery, a hospitalized preterm infant born at 28 weeks or later whose mother lacks immunity, or one born before 28 weeks or weighing 1,000 g or less at birth whatever the mother's immunity: VariZIG (varicella-zoster immune globulin) as soon as possible, within 10 days; the live vaccine is contraindicated in the first two
Aplastic crisis Parvovirus infects red cell precursors, so a child with sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis can develop transient aplastic crisis: falling hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count.
Which vaccine prevents it A face-first maculopapular rash that spreads down is measles or rubella; MMR, a live attenuated vaccine, prevents both: 2 doses, at 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years. Varicella vaccine is also 2 doses, at 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years, so a vaccinated preschooler has had one. Mild itching does not make a rash varicella; varicella needs vesicles in crops.
Common wrong answers Hand-foot-and-mouth disease for itchy crops on the trunk, face and limbs with a normal mouth; it centers on the palms, soles and mouth. Roseola for a toddler with fever and rash; its rash is maculopapular, never vesicular, and comes after the fever breaks. Eczema herpeticum for any vesicular viral rash; it needs atopic dermatitis, and its vesicles are painful and uniform. Rubella for face-first spread; it has no vesicles. Scabies for intense itch; no fever, and it favors finger webs, wrists and periumbilical skin. A travel history is often a decoy when exposure, a single vaccine dose and a classic rash explain the findings. Scalded skin syndrome for peeling; scarlet fever desquamates as it fades, while scalded skin syndrome begins with flaccid bullae in a young child.
Pairs with Acute Rheumatic Fever: Jones criteria, the strep clock, and Lyme arthritis among its mimics. Bruising and Purpura in a Child: IgA vasculitis. Tick-Borne Illness: erythema migrans. Genital Ulcers: the chancre before secondary syphilis. Anaphylaxis: the minutes-not-days reaction. Oral Lesions in a Child: hand-foot-and-mouth disease and the oral vesicles; are the lesions in the mouth, front or back? Congenital Infections (TORCH): parvovirus in pregnancy (hydrops) and congenital rubella. Vaccines in Pregnancy: varicella exposure in a pregnant patient. Seizure with Fever in a Child: the seizure roseola can bring. Atopic Dermatitis: eczema herpeticum. Scabies: the afebrile itchy mimic. Kawasaki Disease: the fever-for-5-days criteria that separate it from scarlet fever; how many days of fever, and is the throat exudative?
Transferable rule

Classify the lesion first (vesicles in crops, maculopapular, lacy, sandpaper, hives), then where it began and whether it came with or after the fever; when joints hurt too, put it on a clock against the exposure. For a varicella exposure, check immunity, then risk group, then the days since exposure (up to 5 for vaccine, 10 for VariZIG).
